claims.claim: The Nile River valley supported early Egyptian civilization because its regular, predictable summer flooding deposited rich sediment that made reliable farming possible, unlike the more destructive floods of Mesopotamia's rivers.

Upper and Lower Egypt were unified under a single ruler around c. 3100 BCE (OpenStax gives c. 3150 BCE); the achievement is credited to a king named Narmer, whom many scholars identify with the figure called Menes.
The Old Kingdom (c. 2613-2181 BCE) was the era of the great stone pyramids; the pyramids at Giza, including the Great Pyramid of Khufu, were built c. 2600-2500 BCE.
Egyptian history is conventionally divided into the Old Kingdom, Middle Kingdom (c. 2040-1782 BCE), and New Kingdom (c. 1570-1069 BCE), separated by Intermediate Periods of weaker central control.
The pharaoh was revered as a god as well as the political and religious head of Egypt, responsible for maintaining ma'at, the principle of order, truth, justice, and balance.
Egyptians developed hieroglyphic writing (c. 3200 BCE), a script combining alphabetic signs, syllabic signs, and word/picture signs; the word means 'sacred writings.'

The Rosetta Stone, a decree of Ptolemy V carved in 196 BCE, carries the same text in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek scripts; discovered in 1799, it let Jean-Francois Champollion announce the decipherment of hieroglyphs on 27 September 1822.
Egyptians practiced mummification because they believed a person was made of several elements, including the ka and ba, that needed the preserved physical body to continue existing in the afterlife.
Egyptian achievements included monumental stone architecture, early surgical medicine, and a 365-day solar calendar of twelve 30-day months plus five extra days, tied to the flooding of the Nile.

New Kingdom pharaohs include Hatshepsut (r. c. 1479-1458 BCE), who expanded trade, and Ramesses II (r. c. 1279-1213 BCE), known for monumental building and a peace treaty following the Battle of Kadesh.
Ancient Egypt was an African civilization along the Nile in northeastern Africa, in sustained contact with Nubia/Kush to the south.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact start dates of Egyptian periods vary between reputable sources.
positions: OpenStax dates the Old Kingdom c. 2613-2181 BCE and unification c. 3150 BCE
Other reference works give the Old Kingdom c. 2686-2181 BCE and unification c. 3100 BCE
conflictingEvidence.resolution: These are scholarly approximations reconstructed from king lists and archaeology; the lesson uses 'c.' throughout, cites the OpenStax figures, and explicitly teaches that such early dates are estimates that differ between sources.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Narmer and Menes are the same person.
positions: Some evidence attributes unification to Narmer
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as OpenStax states: many scholars now believe Narmer and Menes are one and the same, but this is not certain; the lesson does not assert it as settled fact.

sourceRecords.title: Two Hundred Years Ago, the Rosetta Stone Unlocked the Secrets of Ancient Egypt
sourceRecords.notes: Smithsonian Institution magazine feature read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Confirms the stone was erected at an Egyptian temple in 196 BCE during the reign of Ptolemy V; carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, demotic, and ancient Greek; was found in July 1799; and that Champollion announced his decipherment on 27 September 1822. Used to corroborate the Rosetta Stone dates from a museum-institution source. REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Calendar - The Egyptian calendar
sourceRecords.notes: Read via web search result summary on 2026-08-19. Supports: the Egyptian civil calendar of 365 days made of twelve 30-day months plus five added days, among the earliest solar calendars, keyed to the heliacal rising of Sirius (Sothis) that coincided with the Nile flood, and its slow drift because it omitted the extra quarter-day. REFERENCE_ONLY cross-check for the calendar achievement; no wording reproduced.
